responses.final.course_reflection: Doing this lab made me brainstorm some personal project ideas that I could work on. It gave me an idea of how robotics software of robotics works on a surface level. This is something that we often do not think about, as we mainly think about the hardware. Like "An arm that does x", or "a sensor that looks out for y", but we don't think about how that arm will decide how it will move. Or how the data from the sensor will be handled. So because of this, this lab motivated me to want to do more robotics work. The activities we have done in class have also motivated me to want to do more robotics work. For example, watching the video where the blind lady was testing an app made me realise that we could be doing so much more for people with disabilities using technology. And that is where I see most of the value in robotics: aiding humanity. We can use robotics either to do things we cannot do, like fly. But we can also use robotics to help those who cannot do things that we as a human species can already do, like walk. We can take our imagination and think; we can use technology and robotics to help people see, or help a heart pump blood better, in some future where robotics is more advanced. For now, we can help people do simpler things like navigate a building or use a phone (which is what was being done in the video we saw in class).

responses.final.system_synthesis: Robotic hardware is difficult because there are a lot of components that one needs to keep track of in order to achive ones goal. The first one is file structure. In this lab, we were given a repository with all the needed files in their respective places, but organizing your own project is a journey of its own. Then we have the software. I am on a MacBook Pro with an M5 chip, and running Docker, as well as the virtual desktop, makes the laptop hot and the battery drain a bit faster than what I have seen before. This means that you need a relatively powerful machine to be able to run robotics hardware. The architecture that I implemented was a reactive architecture, where the robot constantly reacts to its sensor data. It is like the robot is reacting "live", or on the spot, rather than having a predetermined plan. The ROS 2 middleware is what made this possible by allowing compatible information from the sensors to communicate. We used a LiDAR sensor to read the distance to objects. The sensor then shares information to the /scan topic, because LiDAR publishes to /scan. The obstacle node is another component that processes the sensor data that it receives from /scan by subscribing to /scan. We have function components that make decisions based on the information processed by the nodes, and this occurs because the functions subscribe to the node. The layer that would restrict unsafe motion decision functions, decide_velocity, and front_distance. They set values depending on the readings of the sensor. Since we are dealing with a sensor, we need to consider when the sensor gives us an invalid reading. In our functions, we had safety guards, like if distance == None: return 0.0, to make the velocity 0.0 when we did not know the distance to an object.
